# Molecules From Shared Pairs

## Chlorine: One Shared Pair

Chlorine is 2,8,7, so it has 7 valence electrons and needs 1 more for an octet. Two chlorine atoms each share one electron. That makes one shared pair, and both atoms count it, so each has 8 in its valence shell. This is a single bond, Cl—Cl, in a Cl₂ molecule.

<!-- STEP id="double" -->
## Oxygen: Two Shared Pairs

Oxygen is 2,6, so it needs 2 more electrons. Two oxygen atoms each share two electrons, which makes two shared pairs. This is a **double bond**, drawn with two lines: O=O.

Now you can see why oxygen is written in two ways. O is one atom, and O₂ is the molecule in the air you breathe.

<!-- STEP id="compound" -->
## Different Atoms Share Too

Atoms of two different elements can also share. In **hydrogen chloride**, H—Cl, hydrogen and chlorine each need 1 more electron, so they share one pair.

Oxygen needs 2 but hydrogen needs only 1, so one pair cannot satisfy both. Two hydrogen atoms each share a pair with one oxygen atom, and that gives water, H₂O.

<!-- STEP id="takeaway" -->
## Helium Stays Alone

Not every element forms molecules. A helium atom already has a full K-shell, so its atoms are stable. It exists as single atoms, and neon behaves in the same way.

**Hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, hydrogen chloride and water are all made of molecules held by shared pairs. Salt is not.**
